mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Stopping short leaves the strongest part of the contraction untrained.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Curl your heels as close to your glutes as your range allows.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Lowering too quickly on the way down.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Rushing the lower skips the part of the rep that builds the most control and strength.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Lower under control until your knees are straight.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the weight stack slam down at the bottom.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A slammed stack means gravity did the lowering, not your muscles.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Control the return so the plates settle without banging.

cueHierarchy: Curl by bending at the knees while keeping your hips still.
Feel the back of your thighs work through the rep.
Follow the machine’s guided lever path smoothly and control the weight back to the stack.
Squeeze your hamstrings at the top for a beat.
Lower all the way until your knees are straight each rep.
advancedCoachingNotes: Slow the lowering phase to three counts for extra hamstring tension.
beginnerNotes: Use a light resistance you can curl without your hips lifting.
equipmentSetup: Adjust the seat and any pads so the working joint lines up with the machine’s pivot, set the pin to your working weight, and keep contact with the support pad throughout.

progressionGuidance.progressionReason: Move up to Cable Standing Leg Curl once you can control this one for all your reps.

whyItMatters: The Tibialis Raise builds strength and size in your tibialis anterior. As an isolation movement, it targets those muscles directly to build size and balance.
setupInstructions: Set the balls of your feet on a stable surface with your heels free to drop.
Find a light hold for balance if you need it.
executionSteps: Rise onto the balls of your feet as high as you can.
Pause for a beat at the top.
Lower under control until you feel a full stretch through your calves.
coachingTips: Rise as high onto your toes as possible at the top.
Lower under control into a full stretch at the bottom.
Pause briefly at the top to remove any bounce.
Pull your toes up toward your shin and feel the front of your shin work.
Own the full range of every rep before you add reps or make it harder.
commonMistakes: Bouncing through short, fast reps.
Cutting the stretch short at the bottom.
Letting the ankles roll outward as you rise.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Bouncing through short, fast reps.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Short bounces use the tendon’s spring instead of your calves, so they do less work.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Pause at the top and control a full stretch at the bottom.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Cutting the stretch short at the bottom.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Skipping the stretch removes the part of the range that builds the most.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Let your heels drop below the platform for a full stretch.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Letting the ankles roll outward as you rise.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Rolling out sends force through the outside of your foot instead of your calves.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Drive evenly through your big toe and keep your ankles stacked.

breathingGuidance: Exhale as you rise, breathe in as you lower.
tempoGuidance: Rise with control, pause at the top, then lower slowly.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Move from a deep heel-dropped stretch to a full rise on your toes. Take the tibialis anterior through its full working range each rep.
cueHierarchy: Rise as high onto your toes as possible at the top.
Pull your toes up toward your shin and feel the front of your shin work.
Own the full range of every rep before you add reps or make it harder.
Lower under control into a full stretch at the bottom.
Pause briefly at the top to remove any bounce.
advancedCoachingNotes: Add a two-count pause in the stretched position for extra range.
beginnerNotes: Do the movement on flat ground before adding a deficit or load.
difficultyConsiderations: The Tibialis Raise is an isolation bodyweight movement. You move and stabilise your own bodyweight, so change leverage to progress rather than adding weight. Your hands or feet stay planted, so you move your body against the resistance. Add load gradually as your control improves.
difficultyExplanation: Rated Intermediate because you manage only your own bodyweight, and it works one joint, so it is simpler to learn.

progressionGuidance.regressionReason: Drop back to Tibialis Raise Machine to groove the movement before you add load or complexity.

Start each rep from a controlled, stable position.

Pause briefly where your midsection is working hardest.
Control the return rather than dropping quickly at the end.
coachingTips: Move under control — no yanking or rushing the reps.
Curl your ribs toward your hips rather than pulling with your neck.

Curl your ribs toward your hips and feel your abs shorten.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Pulling on the neck or head to complete the rep.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Pulling your head does the work your abs should, so your midsection gets less out of it.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Rushing through reps with momentum.

mistakeCorrections.correction: Slow each rep down and control both directions.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Arching the lower back away from a braced position.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A loose lower back leaks force and takes the work off your abs.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your ribs down and your midsection tight through the whole rep.

whyItMatters: The Trap Bar Farmer Carry builds strength and size in your forearms, trapezius and rectus abdominis. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Load the sled to a weight you can move steadily and check the surface is clear ahead.
Pick up the load with a flat back and stand tall.
Set your shoulders back and down before you start walking.
executionSteps: Walk with short, deliberate steps while staying tall.
Keep the load from swinging by holding your sides tight.
Set the load down under control at the end of the distance rather than dropping it.
coachingTips: Stand tall and walk with short, controlled steps.
Keep the load steady rather than letting it swing.
Keep your shoulders back and down for the full distance.
Keep a firm grip and let your forearms do the work.

Rounding the shoulders forward under the load.

whyItMatters: The Wide-Grip Lat Pulldown builds strength and size in your latissimus dorsi, biceps and upper back. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Set the pulley to the right height, attach the handle, and step back to remove the slack before your first rep.
Set your grip and start from a full hang or fully stretched position.
Set your shoulders down away from your ears before the first rep.
executionSteps: Drive your elbows down toward your hips.
Pull until your chest reaches your hands.
Lower under control back to a full stretch.
coachingTips: Drive your elbows down toward your hips to lead the pull.
Pull your chest up to your hands rather than leading with your chin.
Start every rep from a full stretch at the top.
Drive your elbows down and back to pull from your lats.
Keep steady tension on the cable through the whole range, including the return.
commonMistakes: Kipping or swinging to complete the rep.
Stopping the pull the moment your chin clears your hands.
Failing to reach a full stretch between reps.
Letting the cable yank your arm back at the end of the rep.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Kipping or swinging to complete the rep.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Swinging uses momentum instead of your back and arms, so the pull does less.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Pull from a dead hang and keep your body quiet.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Stopping the pull the moment your chin clears your hands.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Stopping at the chin trains a shorter range and less of your back.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Pull until your collarbone or chest reaches your hands.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Failing to reach a full stretch between reps.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Without the full stretch you train a shorter range and build less.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Let your arms straighten fully and your shoulder blades rise at the top.

mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Giving in to the cable skips the lowering phase, cutting the work in half.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Control the return against the cable tension rather than giving in to it.

breathingGuidance: Exhale as you pull up, breathe in as you lower under control.
tempoGuidance: Pull with intent, then lower for about two to three counts.
rangeOfMotionNotes: Travel from a full hang to your hands at your chest every rep. Take the latissimus dorsi through its full working range each rep.

Start every rep from a full stretch at the top.

whyItMatters: The Wide-Grip Row builds strength and size in your upper back, biceps, latissimus dorsi and rear deltoids. As a compound movement, it trains several muscles together and carries over to real-world strength and power.
setupInstructions: Set the pulley to the right height, attach the handle, and step back to remove the slack before your first rep.
Set your torso and let your working arm hang with the shoulder blade relaxed forward.
Set a stable base before you begin pulling.
executionSteps: Pull your elbow back toward your hip, leading with the elbow.
Draw the load to your lower ribs and squeeze your shoulder blade back.
Lower under control until your arm is straight and the shoulder blade reaches forward.
coachingTips: Lead with your elbow, not your hand.
Draw the load toward your belt line rather than your chest.
Let your shoulder blade slide back and down at the top of each rep.
Pull with your back and squeeze your shoulder blades together, not just your arms.
Keep steady tension on the cable through the whole range, including the return.
commonMistakes: Yanking with the lower back and using momentum.
Shrugging the shoulder up toward the ear while pulling.
Cutting the stretch short at the bottom.
Letting the cable yank your arm back at the end of the rep.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Yanking with the lower back and using momentum.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Yanking uses your back and momentum instead of the muscles you are rowing with.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your torso still and let your arm and shoulder blade do the work.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Shrugging the shoulder up toward the ear while pulling.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: A shrugging shoulder takes the pull off your back and into your traps.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Keep your shoulder down and pull your elbow straight back.

mistakeCorrections.mistake: Cutting the stretch short at the bottom.
mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Skipping the stretch removes the part of the range that builds the most.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Let your arm fully straighten and your shoulder blade reach forward before the next rep.

mistakeCorrections.whyItMatters: Giving in to the cable skips the lowering phase, cutting the work in half.
mistakeCorrections.correction: Control the return against the cable tension rather than giving in to it.

difficultyExplanation: Rated Beginner because the cable is stable and easy to control, and it coordinates several joints at once.

Press back up until your arms are straight.

Start each rep from a controlled, stable position.

Pause briefly where your midsection is working hardest.
Control the return rather than dropping quickly at the end.
coachingTips: Move under control — no yanking or rushing the reps.
Curl your ribs toward your hips rather than pulling with your neck.
